title: Spring warmth gave no clear catch-share timing link in two English and one Scottish moth sample in 1993-2015
abstract: We split changes in mean May-September moth catch dates into within-taxon timing and catch-share terms. We used consecutive years at the same ECN light trap, with monthly effort weights and common taxa. The main filters kept 46 early and 29 later English pairs, 12 early Scottish pairs, and one later Scottish pair. February-April temperature slopes for the catch-share term were +1.56, -0.35 and -0.15 days per C in the three fitted samples. Their four-test intervals all included zero. The later Scottish sample could not support a model. Mean absolute catch-share terms were 4.48, 5.20 and 3.31 days. They opposed the within-taxon term in 48-59 percent of pairs. Thus catch composition can matter for the date measure, but these data did not establish a repeated spring warmth link to that component. Small samples gave unstable sensitivity fits. Few years, country weather, truncated flight seasons, selected common taxa and weather-dependent capture limit inference. This is an exploratory catch analysis, not a causal climate test. Air pollution and daily extremes were not tested. The package gives code, aggregate results, source hashes, two figures and a retrieval and regeneration method. Source records and derived record tables remain external.

display.caption: Spring temperature slopes for changes in common-taxon mean moth catch dates. The catch-share panel uses four-test intervals. The other panels use twelve-test intervals. The later Scottish sample has one pair and no fitted slope. Few years limit all intervals.
Consecutive year-pairs before and after monthly coverage and common-taxon rules. Later Scottish coverage falls from 13 potential pairs to one main pair. An absent sample is not a zero catch.

Prior ECN night-weather and flight-date results motivate a different catch-composition check. We use no weather adjustment or data table from this publication. Biological source records overlap.
Prior catch-concentration analysis used the same biological archive. We test a different timing component and make no independent-data validation claim.
